sets.name: nationalities
sets.review: Grain holds across the thirteen: 'being from <country> and living there:' then language, holiday, school or civic or everyday, sport or media, politics; the map reads off the set, and the opening echoes western_hemisphere's approved 'being from X ... and at home there'. Agree with the writer's set_review on every point and add: (1) The politics slot comes in three registers, a vote or party pair (nine entries), the leader on the evening news (french, japanese) and the state news (chinese, russian); because french and japanese share the news register, the two state-news entries do not stand apart as a judgement, and the state news is what an insider would say. (2) Emblem check: the footy and the cricket, hockey, Carnival, the Seleção, Christmas markets, the dacha and Sunday lunch are things the person does, not symbols only outsiders hold; none fails the wince test, but brazilian is the one entry carrying both of the outsider's emblems (Carnival and the Seleção), and the Seleção doubles the media slot, so its trim drops it. (3) british is the one entry with a factual wince, GCSEs not being sat in Scotland (edit); 'voting Labour or Tory' is England-weighted too but UK-wide parties and the modal vote, Roger's call. (4) 'English or Spanish at home' is the one language clause whose second language is demographic rather than official or structural; a real particular, kept in the trim; Roger's call. (5) 'Being from X' reads as born there, so a naturalized citizen is american by the notes but not by the opening; the naturalized_citizen role already holds that persona and a map describes the modal member; fine. (6) Density: five entries carry six particulars (australian, brazilian, german, italian, nigerian) against five for the rest; the trims even this out. (7) Eleven of thirteen are over 32 words; trims supplied, a micro-trim where one or two words suffice (american, australian, chinese, german, italian, nigerian) and a slot dropped where three are needed (brazilian, indian, japanese, russian); british's edit is 30 words on its own. (8) The label appears mid-sentence as the language in japanese, russian, german, italian and french ('Japanese at home'); that is content, not the opening repetition rule 1 forbids. (9) Seleção, maturità and rentrée would be the first accented letters in any corpus description (today the only non-ASCII characters are em-dashes and techno_hierophantic's symbols); harmless, noted for Roger.

sets.name: ethnic and racial memberships
sets.review: Grain holds across the seven and is plainly different from the nationalities: 'having roots in <region>:' then the family's languages with 'or only English', one custom, and 'living anywhere from <home city> to <diaspora city>' (against 'from <country> and living there'). Agree with the writer's set_review, including the template break for the two indigenous entries ('roots in the Americas' would admit everyone from the hemisphere; 'being Navajo, Maya, Quechua or another of the Americas' first peoples' and 'being Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander' are the right openings) and the absence of a history clause on african (rule 8: plainly and stop; a slave-trade clause is an outsider's framing that most of the members at home have no part in). Add: (1) Two edits of one kind, an entry naming a group that the next clause leaves out: middle_eastern names Persian and gives 'Eid or Easter' (add Nowruz); south_asian names Bangladesh and omits Bengali (add it). (2) 'Or only English' is the assimilated-diaspora clause and is Anglocentric: the largest African diaspora is Brazil (Portuguese), the largest Maghrebi diaspora is France, Haitians and Cubans speak Kreyòl and Spanish, Argentines of Italian heritage Spanish. The corpus is English and the persona answers in English, so it is defensible as written; Roger's call whether african and middle_eastern get 'or only English or French'. (3) The custom slot takes the modal member every time (church or mosque; New Year; Christmas; Eid, Easter, Nowruz; Diwali, Eid, Vaisakhi; the ceremonies; mob, country and kin) and so excludes a secular or minority-faith member in each case (a secular African, a Jewish European, a Christian or Sikh Indian); writer 2's religion entries carry the faith axis separately, so this is the right design; the thinnest customs are 'New Year with the family' (east_asian) and 'the ceremonies' (indigenous_american), both kept. (4) 'On the reservation' is US usage (Canada: reserve; Latin America: comunidad, pueblo) in an entry that names Maya and Quechua; the label 'indigenous american' is itself US-and-Canada demographic usage, so the clause is coherent with it, and the pan-Americas alternative costs words; Roger's call. (5) Hebrew and Passover stay out of middle_eastern, as the writer did; by speakers Hebrew is behind Kurdish and Amazigh, also out, and the jewish entry carries a Mizrahi persona; agree. (6) A gap in the queue, not the drafts: there is no hispanic or latino entry; under the heritage framing a Latin American is european, indigenous_american and african in mixture, and brazilian is in the other map, but US demographic practice treats Hispanic as an ethnicity; for Roger to decide whether the map wants it. (7) By design the heritage entries will all load on the existing rooted trait ('keeping their language, food and holidays close'), since their three slots are rooted's three nouns; the difference is attitude against membership, as the writer's nearest_existing says. (8) Five of seven are over 32 words; trims supplied; the indigenous_american trim keeps all three slots by dropping 'living' (the alternative, dropping 'the ceremonies', leaves two slots); the south_asian trim opens on 'the subcontinent', the notes' own word.

summary: Twenty drafts read against packet_5b.md and entries_5b_maps.json: 17 ok, 3 edit, each a named group the next clause left out (british: GCSEs are not sat in Scotland, drop the doubled school clause, 30 words; middle_eastern: Nowruz beside Eid and Easter, since Persian is named; south_asian: Bengali, since Bangladesh is named). Form passes everywhere (no label in the opening, one sentence, US spelling, inside voice), nearest_existing is plausible for all twenty with no duplicate in the corpus, and both maps hold one grain; I agree with both set_reviews. The emblems (footy, hockey, Carnival, the Seleção, Christmas markets, the dacha, Sunday lunch) pass as lived particulars, brazilian being the one entry carrying two outsider emblems; the state news is the honest politics for chinese and russian, and french and japanese share a leader-on-the-news register. Sixteen drafts over 32 words carry trim_to_32 (a micro-trim where one or two words suffice, a slot dropped otherwise; for the three edits it trims the edited text); 'ok' with a non-empty issues list means seedable as drafted, the listed points being Roger's calls: 'English or Spanish' (keep), 'church or mosque every week', 'on the reservation', european's Christmas, the Anglocentric 'or only English', and the missing hispanic/latino entry.
